title: Past-paper walkthroughs
summary: Guided walkthroughs of the 2026 Prelim by domain, its long problem-solving scenarios, the code-reading MCQs of the 2026 Final, and the 2025 MCQs, with the pattern behind each question and the anatomy of its distractors.
syllabus: NOAI 2026 Preliminary Round (300 MCQs) by domain

lessons.title: 2026 Prelim: Mathematics and Computing
lessons.summary: Every question pattern from the maths and computing sections, solved with the fastest method.
objectives: You can solve each recurring maths and computing question pattern within the time budget
You can link each pattern to its lesson

concepts.name: Pattern catalogue
concepts.explain: The 2026 Prelim reused a small number of templates: shape rules, norms, dot products, matrix properties, derivative facts, descriptive statistics, metric formulas, optimiser definitions, Python output prediction, NumPy syntax, PyTorch API purposes and error causes. Recognising the template is half the answer.
concepts.analogy: Like recognising question types in a Ten-Year Series book.

visual.shows: About 25 cards, one per question template, each with the template name, a real 2026 item number, the fastest method, the usual trap and the linked lesson.
visual.interaction: Filter cards by domain and subtopic; flip a card to see the method; shuffle mode deals a fresh variant of a random template to solve in 20 seconds.
visual.aha: A few dozen templates cover most questions.

concepts.name: Seven model solutions against the clock
concepts.explain: Seven real 2026 Prelim items are solved in full, each with a target time: Q1 (shape of a 3×2 times 2×4 product, 10 s), Q15 (eigenvalues [4, 2, 0] mean singular, 15 s), Q34 (sigmoid derivative, 15 s), Q54 (z-score, 15 s), Q74 (Newton profiling: inverting the 10K × 10K Hessian, 30 s), Q99 (selecting a pandas column whose name has a space, 15 s) and Q115 (calling backward twice accumulates gradients, 15 s). Each solution names the single fact the item tests and the trap behind each wrong option.
concepts.analogy: Like having a tutor talk through each question with you.

visual.shows: Each of the seven questions as it appears in the paper with a countdown set to its target time; after you answer, steps reveal the fastest method, the one fact it relies on, the misconception behind each wrong option and a link to the lesson that teaches it.
visual.interaction: Answer under the countdown; reveal the steps one at a time; mark a question 'review again' to send it to your error log.
visual.aha: Most maths and computing items fall in about 15 seconds once you know the one fact they test, which banks time for the scenario questions.

checkpoint_focus: 2026 Prelim maths items: shapes, norms, determinants, eigenvalues, derivatives, probability, optimisers
2026 Prelim computing items: Python output prediction, NumPy shapes, pandas, PyTorch

lessons.title: 2026 Prelim: AI/ML/DL and Generative AI
lessons.summary: Definitions, architectures and model-behaviour questions from the AI and GenAI sections, and how their distractors are built.
objectives: You can map each AI and GenAI question to its concept cluster
You can explain the key fact behind each answer
You can name the trap in each distractor

concepts.name: Recall clusters
concepts.explain: These sections cluster around: classical ML definitions, bias-variance and regularisation, ensembles, NN components and training tricks, CNN and detection/segmentation terms, NLP and transformer facts, LLM decoding and adaptation, diffusion and multimodal models.
concepts.analogy: Like grouping vocabulary words by theme so they are easier to remember.

visual.shows: A map of concept clusters sized by how many 2026 questions they had, each linking to its questions.
visual.interaction: Click a cluster to practise its questions in a quick-fire round.
visual.aha: Exam weight is concentrated in identifiable clusters.

concepts.name: Seven model solutions across the clusters
concepts.explain: One real 2026 Prelim item per cluster, solved in full: Q155 (boosting reduces bias), Q176 (Xavier initialisation suits tanh and sigmoid), Q204 (stacked 3×3 convolutions), Q213 (BERT versus GPT), Q235 (LoRA), Q245 (DDPM as a Markov chain with a learnt reverse process) and Q254 (cross-attention between modalities). Each solution states the key fact, the confusable pair behind the distractors, and the lesson that teaches it.
concepts.analogy: Like having a tutor talk through each question with you.

visual.shows: The seven items as they appear in the paper; after answering, a reveal shows the key fact, the confusable pair (for example bagging versus boosting, encoder versus decoder) and a link to the teaching lesson.
visual.interaction: Answer first; reveal the steps one at a time; tag each miss with its cluster so the error log groups them.
visual.aha: Recall items are won or lost on one confusable pair, so learn the pairs, not isolated definitions.

concepts.name: Distractor anatomy
concepts.explain: Wrong options are built from common misconceptions: a squared value instead of its root, the opposite effect, a correct fact that does not answer the question, or a confusion between similar terms (precision versus recall, BatchNorm versus LayerNorm). Naming the misconception behind each distractor strengthens your understanding.
concepts.analogy: Learning a magician's tricks so you are never fooled by them again.

visual.shows: A question with each option colour-tagged by misconception type and a short note on why someone might pick it.
visual.interaction: Click options to reveal their misconception; filter questions by misconception type.
visual.aha: Distractors are predictable, and recognising their patterns protects you from them.

checkpoint_focus: Confusable pairs (e.g. bagging vs boosting, BERT vs GPT)

lessons.title: 2026 Prelim: Problem-solving scenarios
lessons.summary: Long scenario questions about training logs, metrics and systems, with a reading method that saves time.
objectives: You can read a scenario question stem-first and extract the key numbers
You can map a scenario to a known diagnosis pattern
You can name the keyword that decides a scenario (e.g. oscillating loss → learning rate)

concepts.name: Stem-first reading
concepts.explain: Read the final question line first, then scan the scenario for the numbers it needs (train vs validation gap, class ratio, learning rate, memory). Most scenario options are long; compare them on the one fact that differs.
concepts.analogy: Like reading the question before the comprehension passage in an English paper.

visual.shows: A long scenario with the question line, key numbers and distractor differences highlighted step by step.
visual.interaction: Step through highlighting; then try the next scenario yourself with a highlighter tool.
visual.aha: Scenario questions test one diagnosis hidden among many details.

concepts.name: Case studies
concepts.explain: Six real 2026 Prelim scenarios, each mapped to its diagnosis: Q258 (50 patients and 100 biomarkers: overfitting because p > n), Q265 (fraud after class weights: recall matters most when a missed fraud is costly), Q272 (NaN at epoch 23: anomaly detection and activation statistics before guessing), Q273 (validation stuck at 10% on 10 classes: a label-mapping bug), Q274 (out of memory at batch 128: accumulation plus checkpointing) and Q283 (GPT-2-scale divergence: learning-rate warm-up).

visual.shows: Each case as a patient chart: symptoms (the numbers from the stem), the four options as candidate diagnoses, the decisive evidence highlighted, and the eliminated options crossed out with a one-line reason.
visual.interaction: At each decision point choose a diagnosis before the evidence is revealed; choices are scored and misses are added to the error log.
visual.aha: Scenarios repeat a small set of diagnoses.

concepts.name: Keyword triggers
concepts.explain: Long scenario questions usually hinge on one or two keywords. 'Oscillates wildly' points to the learning rate, 'CUDA out of memory' to batch size and precision, '1% positives' to precision and recall, and 'p > n' to overfitting. 'Validation at 10% on 10 classes' points to a label or pipeline bug, and '2023 data, tested in 2024' to drift.
concepts.analogy: A doctor who hears 'chest pain and sweating' immediately thinks of a short list of causes.

visual.shows: A network linking scenario keywords to concepts and to the lessons that cover them.
visual.interaction: Click a keyword to highlight its concepts; play a quiz that shows a stem and asks which keyword decides it.
visual.aha: Spotting the decisive keyword is the fastest route through long scenario questions.

checkpoint_focus: Stem-first reading of 2026 Prelim scenario items
Keyword triggers: oscillation, OOM, 1% positives, p > n, chance-level accuracy, drift

lessons.title: 2026 Final MCQs and the 2025 paper
lessons.summary: The 20 code-reading MCQs of the 2026 Final, the 20 definition-level 2025 MCQs, and what the trend says about 2027.
objectives: You can find the faulty line in a 15 to 30 line code snippet
You can explain each 2026 Final MCQ with its concept and line
You can describe how question style changed from 2025 to 2026

concepts.name: Code-reading patterns
concepts.explain: Final MCQs show 15 to 30 lines of code and ask which line must change, what the bug is or which option is correct. Patterns: sign or formula errors (AdaBoost weights, positional encoding), wrong normalisation (sqrt(d_k), loss / accumulation_steps), leakage (selection outside CV), wrong function choice (softmax for multi-label), state bugs (optimiser registration, BatchNorm running stats), and edge cases (IoU union == 0, truncating EOS).
concepts.analogy: Like proofreading: you are hunting for one wrong word in a paragraph.

visual.shows: Each Final code snippet with clickable lines; picking a line shows whether it holds the issue and why.
visual.interaction: Click the suspicious line before revealing the options; then answer the MCQ.
visual.aha: Most code MCQs hinge on one line and one concept.

concepts.name: Five Final MCQs read line by line
concepts.explain: Five 2026 Final MCQs are read the way an examiner wrote them: Q3 (feature selection must sit inside the cross-validation loop), Q5 (the sign of the AdaBoost weight update), Q8 (BatchNorm running statistics stored as buffers), Q10 (dividing the loss by accumulation_steps) and Q18 (truncation removes <EOS>). For each, find the decisive line, name the concept, then eliminate the options.
concepts.analogy: Like a post-mortem after a match.

visual.shows: The code snippet with line numbers, the four options, and a reasoning trail that highlights the lines in the order an expert reads them, the concept each relies on, and why each wrong option fails, with links to the teaching lessons.
visual.interaction: Click the line you suspect before seeing the options; then choose an option; reveal the reasoning trail one step at a time and compare your line with the decisive one.
visual.aha: Code MCQs reward reading the one decisive line against a formula you know, not pattern-matching the options.

concepts.name: The 2025 MCQs and cross-year trends
concepts.explain: The 2025 MCQs were definition-level: unsupervised learning, bagging, RL, underfitting, boosting, optimisers, vanishing gradients, early stopping, residuals, schedules, pooling, YOLO, RPN, depthwise convolutions, Mask R-CNN, attention, BERT, beam search, CLS, causal masking. 2025 had one 2.5-hour round. 2026 added a 300-question Prelim and made the Final MCQs code-heavy. 2027 halves the Prelim to 150 questions at the same pace. Concepts examined every year (attention, regularisation, ensembles, CNN basics, metrics) are the safest bets.
concepts.analogy: Like reading weather patterns over several years before planning an outdoor event.

visual.shows: A heat map with subtopics as rows and the three papers (2025 MCQ, 2026 Prelim, 2026 Final MCQ) as columns, each cell showing its question count: for example training and regularisation 3, 23 and 4; CNNs and vision 5, 23 and 2; PyTorch 0, 24 and 2; NLP and Transformers 4, 12 and 4.
visual.interaction: Hover a cell to list its questions; sort rows by total or by any one paper; click a row to open the lessons that teach it.
visual.aha: Frequently examined subtopics deserve the most revision time.

checkpoint_focus: Sign and formula errors, wrong normalisation, wrong dim
